doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: The 1983 Motown album Bobby M. Blow and doubts about funk
summary: Lenny White turned his fusion tunes into R&B; he did well but did not want a funk career, and sings only a tune or two a set.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Musically never. I’ve left things that I didn’t like, but musically never, I’ve never had one go bad on me or one that I couldn’t do, whether it was R&B, funk, whatever it was, I could still do it. But preference now is bop, or getting a little out here and there, but the preference is bop. But no I’ve never had anything go bad. When I did the album on Motown in ’83, it was Bobby M. Blow, it was a funk R&B record. And when I first got the contract when Rick got me that contract, I had all these grandiose ideas of my fusion band being — recording my fusion band. And then Lenny White became the producer, which worked out for me, and we took all those fusion tunes and turned them into R&B. And I saw the writing on the wall and actually at one point my brother, we were in the studio here in Buffalo just working on the tunes and making the transitions. And at one point I went outside and I was almost having like a panic attack, and I started crying, telling my brother, I says, “I don’t think this is right.” I know the truth of the matter is Motown won’t know what to do with a jazz product, a fusion jazz even product, they won’t know what to do with it because they don’t have anything like it on their label. So I’ll give them something and it could be wonderful and then it will probably do nothing. But if I give it an R&B touch then they can deal with it, I mean they can put it out. So I know the business of what I’m talking about. But I feel like I’m bastarding my craft. I’ve worked for two and a half years on this book of tunes and they’re great. I went with the business decision. We’re going to go the whole way. We’re going to switch it over and

make it R&B and I’m going to blow funky, less notes, do the whole bit. And it did very well actually. But my brother could never understand this in my nature, but I didn’t want to do a second, they didn’t pick up a second anyways, but I wouldn’t have done a second. And I decided, and my brother says, “You could be rich, I mean you could do this well.” I says, “I know I could do it well but now that I’ve done it I have to do it because that’s what the people hear, the record. So now I have to play that. But I don’t want to play that anymore. Once in a while I like it. One tune, cool. Two tunes, cool. Because I enjoy playing funk. But as a career? No. He says, “Yeah but—” “No you don’t understand. It’s got nothing to do with the money, Michael, you don’t play jazz for the money.” And he just couldn’t see that. I sing very well, I’m lucky, but I sing very well and I got a kind of a style from Mark Murphy and Carmen McRae and I kind of meshed together. And every time I sing people flip. But I’ll only sing one tune a set. Maybe two at the most, but most of the time just one tune a set, or I sing at weddings when I do weddings with my friends I sing Sinatra tunes and Swing stuff. Well without fail, I mean people have offered to back me on a record where I sing, and my brother says, “You’ve got to sing more tunes in the set and you know you draw more people.” “Michael, if I do that then I become the singer that plays saxophone.” I says, “That’s not what I want to be. I want to play my horn.” You know, so don’t—
